DESIGN & INSPECTION · POSTED SEP 17, 2026 · 5 MIN READ

GD&T starts with
function, not symbols.

Geometric dimensioning and tolerancing communicates how much variation a part can accept and how its important features relate to one another. The clearest drawings begin with function.

Why use geometric tolerances?

Size dimensions answer questions such as how wide a slot is. They do not always describe whether the slot is straight, perpendicular to a face, or correctly located relative to other features. GD&T adds controls for form, orientation, location, and runout so the drawing can describe the relationships that matter to assembly and operation.

Begin with how the part works

Before adding symbols, identify the features that locate, support, mate with, or move against other parts. Those functional relationships guide the datum reference frame. A datum is a theoretically exact reference; a datum feature is the real surface or feature used to establish that reference during measurement or assembly.

A primary, secondary, and tertiary datum sequence constrains the part in a repeatable order. The order should reflect how the part is mounted or used, rather than simply following whichever edges are easiest to dimension.

Read the feature control frame as a complete instruction

A feature control frame names a geometric characteristic, states its tolerance, and may reference datums. The tolerance defines an acceptable zone around the ideal geometry. For a hole pattern, a position control can define where each hole’s axis may lie relative to the selected datum reference frame.

Material condition modifiers can change how a tolerance applies as a feature’s actual size changes. Their use affects functional allowance and inspection, so they should be selected intentionally and interpreted under the drawing’s governing standard.

Connect the drawing to inspection

A useful control should be measurable. Ask how the part will be fixtured, what datum simulators or probes will establish the references, and which measurement method is appropriate. Coordinate measuring machines, functional gages, and other methods each answer different questions and have different uncertainty and setup considerations.

A practical review checklist

  • Can a reviewer tell which surfaces locate the part in use?
  • Do the datum references reflect the assembly sequence?
  • Does each tolerance control a real functional requirement?
  • Can manufacturing and quality teams inspect the requirement consistently?
  • Are the units, modifiers, and governing standard clear?

GD&T works best as a shared design language. A small amount of functional thinking before drawing release can prevent ambiguous notes and mismatched inspection setups later.

Further reading

  • ASME Y14.5 — Dimensioning and Tolerancing
